sentences.text: The largest known skull of Purussaurus brasiliensis measures up to 1.4 meters in length from the snout tip to the quadrates, which are the bones at the back of the skull base.
Its teeth were consistently around 50 mm long and curved slightly backwards across all three species, being taller and more pointed at the front while lower and more rounded at the back.
While the Venezuelan species possessed a flattened skull much more than the other two, P. mirandai would measure around 10 meters in length.
Its large body size and wide skull suggest a lifestyle that was mostly aquatic.

Some paleontologists estimate the full body length of P. brasiliensis was between 11 and 13 meters, making Purussaurus one of the largest known crocodiles, and some estimates suggest it might be the largest crocodyliform to have ever existed.
A 2015 study estimated the bite force of Purussaurus at around 69,000 Newtons, or approximately 7 metric tons-force.
Purussaurus was perhaps capable of overpowering even the large mammals of its time.
The genus Purussaurus was first described by Rodrigues in 1892, and the type species, P. brasiliensis, was described by Barbosa-Rodrigues in the same year.
New Purussaurus fossils were found in the Peruvian Amazon in 2005 by the Franco-Peruvian Fitzcarrald expedition.
The name Purussaurus combines the Purus River where fossils were found and the Greek word for 'reptile' or 'lizard'.
Purussaurus had all sense organs at the top of its head, indicating it was an ambush predator similar to modern caimans.
Ridges on Purussaurus teeth indicate it hunted large vertebrates by puncturing and holding flesh, as the teeth are curved slightly backward, pointing toward the inside of the mouth.

Biomechanical models indicate Purussaurus could perform the 'death roll' maneuver to subdue and dismember prey, a capability supported by biomechanical analyses of skulls indicating it and Deinosuchus may have been capable of performing the 'death roll' maneuver.

Purussaurus was an apex predator capable of hunting a wide range of prey due to its large size and strength, and adult Purussaurus preyed on large vertebrates like xenarthrans, notoungulates, and giant turtles, facing little competition from smaller carnivores.
Purussaurus likely ate Stupendemys turtles, various crocodilians, birds, and mammals including sloths, bats, capybara-like rodents up to 700 kg, primates, and river dolphins.
Bite marks on a phorusrhacid tibia suggest it may have been killed by a young Purussaurus, though whether this was scavenging or active predation is debated.
Researchers suggest that Purussaurus's large size may have made it vulnerable to environmental changes, favoring smaller, more resilient species.
Purussaurus is classified within the family Alligatoridae and belongs to the subfamily Caimaninae, where it is currently classified as a giant representative of the subfamily Caimaninae.
Purussaurus has two direct parent taxa in its classification hierarchy.
Purussaurus lived in South America between 16 and 5.3 million years ago during the Miocene period, inhabiting environments including rivers, floodplains, and lakes.
Purussaurus lived in the Americas during the Miocene epoch, specifically from the Friasian to the Huayquerian stages, and P. brasiliensis originates from the Miocene of Brazil.

Some studies suggest Purussaurus may have been heavier than Sarcosuchus or Deinosuchus due to its broader snout requiring a stronger neck, and it is debated whether additional traces on bones of Xenastrapotherium kraglievichi represent scavenging by a crocodyliform similar to Langstonia.
